claims.text: The as-deposited high-entropy-alloy coating has a dual-phase FCC/BCC microstructure with a characteristic phase-boundary distribution.
A controlled heat treatment can alter the FCC/BCC phase volume fraction.
A controlled heat treatment can increase or decrease the density of FCC/BCC interfaces.
Sustained loading at elevated temperature promotes creep deformation in the coating.
FCC/BCC phase boundaries hinder dislocation glide under sustained loading.
FCC/BCC phase boundaries hinder dislocation climb under sustained loading.
Phase-boundary pinning is the primary governing factor for the coating's creep resistance.
A high density of FCC/BCC phase boundaries pins dislocations.
Pinning-induced suppression of dislocation climb and glide reduces the creep rate.
Samples with an increased density of well-distributed phase boundaries will have lower creep rates than the as-deposited baseline.
Samples with reduced phase-boundary density will undergo faster progressive plastic deformation than the baseline.
The proposed pinning effect operates under sustained stress and elevated temperatures where creep is activated.
The proposed pinning effect will not govern at extreme conditions where other degradation mechanisms dominate.
Dynamic strain aging and precipitate strengthening are plausible alternative contributors to creep resistance.
The relative contributions of phase-boundary pinning and alternative mechanisms may vary with temperature and loading conditions.
Failure of increased boundary density to reduce creep rate significantly, or failure of reduced boundary density to increase creep rate, would falsify phase-boundary pinning as the governing factor.
